results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve); kFLC index accepted as an alternative to CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting MRI markers; additional supporting evidence recommended in people over 50 or with vascular risk factors.

results.key_findings: NMOSD with AQP4-IgG requires one core clinical characteristic (optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem, diencephalic or cerebral syndrome) and a positive cell-based AQP4-IgG assay; seronegative NMOSD requires additional clinical and MRI criteria.
results.title: International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics

Do not attribute the cord and cerebellar findings to vitamin B12 deficiency on a low-normal B12 of 228 pg/mL: subacute combined degeneration does not produce enhancing brain lesions or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands
Do not attribute the left arm symptoms to cervical radiculopathy: the loss is not dermatomal and comes with dorsal column and pyramidal signs and a C3-C4 cord lesion
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Reyes is a 32-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman, a school teacher, who presents to the emergency department with an 8-day history of progressive left arm numbness and worsening gait unsteadiness. Eight days ago she noticed tingling and numbness in her left arm, starting at the shoulder and spreading distally to the hand over 2-3 days. She describes the sensation as persistent pins and needles, worst over the dorsum of the left hand and forearm, non-positional, unrelated to neck position at the time of onset. Over the same period she began to notice difficulty with left-hand fine motor tasks: fumbling when buttoning her daughter's clothing and dropping objects she was holding. Concurrently, her gait has become progressively unsteady. She reports feeling like she is walking on a boat, with a tendency to veer to the left, and she has had to widen her stance to avoid falling. She tripped twice on flat ground over the past 3 days. This morning she noticed that neck flexion causes an electric shock-like sensation that shoots into her left arm and left leg, prompting her husband to bring her to the emergency department. On further questioning, she reports that approximately 11 months ago she developed tingling and numbness in the left arm lasting about 3 weeks, which was attributed by her primary care physician to a pinched nerve in her neck; no imaging was performed and the episode resolved spontaneously. She also describes unexplained fatigue disproportionate to her activity level for the past 6-8 months, and she noticed that her walking became noticeably worse after climbing the stairs at school or after a hot shower during the current episode. She denies visual loss, eye pain, diplopia, facial numbness, difficulty swallowing, hearing changes, bladder or bowel incontinence, fever, weight loss, joint pain, skin rashes, oral ulcers, dry eyes, or dry mouth. She has no history of seizures or head trauma. There is no family history of neurological disease.
